newsitem.title: Italy: Food summit ends with call for action on words.
newsitem.headline: Food summit ends with call for action on words.

text.p: A U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit closed on Sunday with ringing calls to end hunger but with deep differences about how to do it, highlighted by U.S. reservations over a blueprint for feeding the planet.

The five-day summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Rome, overshadowed by the refugee crisis in Zaire, was the highest level meeting of its kind called to discuss efforts to end starvation.
It adopted a Declaration on World Food Security and Plan of Action which pledge to halve the number of hungry people from the current 840 million by the year 2015.

"We have the possibiity to do it, we have the knowhow, we have the resources (and) we have shown that we have the will. Let's now run against time and go beyond the set goal," FAO director general Jacques Diouf told the closing session.

The summit had shown that "all together we will work hand in hand to ensure that young children and babies will not cry of hunger and that mothers will not be looking at children who have no hope," Diouf, who is from Senegal, told delegates.
The summit's chairman, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, called the non-binding agreements a milestone.
"Before the eyes of the world you made a public commitment," he said. "I hope we will never forget our commitment."

The summit texts were adopted by acclamation at the start of the gathering after more than two years of negotiation and contain compromise language in contentious areas such as trade, development aid, population, sanctions and women's rights.
In a sign of abiding fundamental differences, 15 delegations lodged reservations or interpretations on the texts, including the United States, the world's biggest single food aid provider.

It noted that it had not agreed to a target of spending 0.7 percent of annual economic wealth on development aid and took issue with a reaffirmation by the summit of the "right of everyone to have access to safe and nutritious food".

"The United States believes that the attainment of any "right to adequate food' or "fundamental right to be free from hunger' is a goal or aspiration to be realised progressively that does not give rise to any international obligations nor diminish the responsibilities of national governments toward their citizens," the U.S. statement said.

Washington, which led rich nations in calls in Rome to make free trade the key to ending the poverty at the root of hunger, fears recognition of a "right to food" could lead to lawsuits from poor nations seeking aid and special trade provisions.

Neither President Bill Clinton nor most other leaders of industrialised nations took part in the summit, which fell far short of Diouf's stated aim of bringing together some 100 of the world's heads of state and government.
"That was not a particularly comforting thing," South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told reporters.

Cuba's veteran communist leader Fidel Castro, the star summiteer in a depleted field, used his speech on Saturday to lash out at capitalism, slamming the agreed goals of the gathering as modest and cosmetic.
"Let the truth prevail and not hypocrisy and deceit," said Castro, who is scheduled to remain in Rome for an historic meeting with Pope John Paul on Tuesday.
Castro's reference to food as a "human right" was echoed by many leaders of Third World countries and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) which met on the sidelines of the summit.

An NGO representative, Jeanot Minla Mfou'ou of Cameroon, told the closing summit session that the world had to choose between "profit for a few or food for all". "Food is a fundamental and unquestionable human right," he said.
The summit was the last in a series of major U.N. conferences over the past four years to map out an agenda for tackling the world's problems on the eve of the 21st century.

Diouf was adamant at the outset that it should not re-open policy wounds on sensitive issues such as how to respond to a booming world population, the cause of a bitter row between the Vatican and Washington in 1994 at a U.N. conference in Cairo.

The Vatican was joined by several delegations in Rome, including Argentina and many Moslem states, in reaffirming objections to language on population and family planning in the food summit documents, which repeat the Cairo agreement.
